newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan economy seen chugging along gently.
newsitem.headline: Japan economy seen chugging along gently.

text.p: The weaker yen will keep the Japanese economy chugging along gently this business year and help it pick up steam in the next, a Reuters poll of economists released on Thursday showed.

Analysts said the economy would be burdened by tax increases and was unlikely to be blessed with government stimulus measures in fiscal 1997/98 but the yen's depreciation over the past year would offset some of the pain.
"It will be sustained although not eye-catching growth," said Susumu Kato, chief economist at BZW Securities.
Predictions from 32 economists produced an average forecast of 1.7 percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP) for the business year that began on April 1.
Forecasts ranged from 0.7 percent to 3.5 percent, with most economists revising their forecasts up slightly from the previous survey in January.
The survey was conducted from April 1 to April 4 and covered 33 brokerages and research bodies, although not all those polled responded to all the questions.
"It's the lower yen, you can't ignore its effects," said Junji Ota, research supervisor at Okasan Research Institute.

Since soaring to a post-war high of 79.75 to the dollar in April 1995, the yen tumbled steadily, making Japanese exports cheaper overseas. Large manufacturers, which aggressively restructured during the high-yen period, have benefitted and shown improved corporate profits.
The yen was trading at about 127 in early afternoon trade on Thursday.
While most economists predicted a gradual rise of the yen against the dollar towards the end of the year, they said the recent falls would still help the economy early next year.
"The time lag between an actual weakening in the yen and and when its appears in the economy is about five quarters," said Russell Jones, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Japan.
Low stock levels and an upturn in the labour market are also expected to underpin the recovery, economists said.
The inventory-to-sales ratio for Japanese firms has been falling steadily, which should encourage firms to keep industry output at healthy levels.
Meanwhile, bonuses and wages are higher and the number of employed has grown by over one million in the last year, with the last few months, in particular, showing large increases.

But with the economy's return to recovery -- it is expected have grown by over 2.5 percent in fiscal 1996/97 -- the government has turned its attention from stimulus efforts to cutting the budget deficit and increasing taxes.
On April 1 the sales tax was raised to five percent from three percent and special income tax cuts were abolished -- moves seen by some as threatening to growth.

Consumption is widely expected to plunge for several months at the beginning of the business year -- as consumers recover after heavy spending ahead of the sales tax rise on larger purchases, such as cars and housing.

But many economists said they expect spending to recover in the second half of the business year and gather strength in fiscal 1998/99. Twenty-two forecasts produced a mean average prediction of 2.7 percent GDP growth for that year.
But not all were optimistic about future spurts of growth down the track.

"There's a lot more risk of negative surprises further along," said Shunsuke Motani of Sphynx Investment Research, adding that he expected a slowdown in the United States in the second half of this business year to take the bounce out of Japanese exports.
